question:
The predictive ability of a polygenic score, measured by variance explained, is necessarily lower than the SNP heritability for the phenotype. Answer with one of the following:
True
False

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that is tagged by (and thus in principle explainable by) the measured SNPs. A polygenic score is simply a linear combination of those same SNPs; with perfect effect-size estimates (i.e., infinite GWAS sample size and no stratification or other biases) the score recovers exactly that variance. Therefore the predictive R² of a PGS is bounded above by, but is not necessarily strictly below, SNP heritability. In finite samples the R² is almost always lower, yet the word “necessarily” makes the claim false.

(The claim would be true if it said “cannot exceed” rather than “necessarily lower.”)

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability (h²_SNP) is the theoretical upper bound on variance that can be captured by additive effects of the measured SNPs. A polygenic score constructed from those same SNPs can, in the limit of infinite training data and optimal weighting (e.g., via BLUP or perfect posterior means), recover essentially all of that variance; nothing in the definitions forces the out-of-sample R² to be strictly smaller. In finite samples the achieved R² is lower, but the statement claims “necessarily,” which is not true.

4.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True. Polygenic scores are derived from finite GWAS summary statistics and thus rely on estimated effect sizes for a finite set of SNPs; even in the limit of perfect tagging, shrinkage, winner’s curse, and imperfect linkage disequilibrium mean that the out-of-sample variance captured by the score is strictly less than the total SNP-heritability estimated from the same set of variants.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance captured by the best linear predictor that uses all SNPs (i.e., the population value of \(R^2\) attainable with the true SNP effect sizes). Any polygenic score is constructed from estimated rather than known effect sizes; the resulting out-of-sample \(R^2\) is therefore strictly less than \(h^2_{SNP}\) except in the asymptotic limit of infinite, perfectly matched samples. Hence the predictive ability of a PGS, measured by variance explained, is necessarily lower than SNP heritability.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance captured by the optimal linear combination of all SNPs (i.e., the best linear predictor). A polygenic score is a linear predictor whose weights are estimated from finite data; the resulting estimation error in the weights guarantees that its out-of-sample \(R^2\) cannot reach this theoretical maximum. Hence the predictive \(R^2\) is necessarily strictly lower than SNP heritability. (Only in the unattainable limit of infinite, perfectly ascertained samples could equality hold.)

Final answer: True

4.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: C4 and C6 have the stronger reading here. While the mathematical limit of infinite, perfectly matched data is a useful theoretical benchmark, the statement uses “necessarily” in the context of how polygenic scores are actually constructed and evaluated. Estimation error, imperfect LD tagging, shrinkage toward zero, and unavoidable sample mismatch are not optional add-ons; they are baked into every real PGS pipeline. Those features guarantee that the realized out-of-sample R² falls short of the SNP-heritability ceiling estimated from the same SNPs. C3 and C5 correctly note that equality is admissible in an idealized limit, yet that limit is unreachable with any finite GWAS we can ever run or validate. Therefore the strict inequality asserted by the claim holds in every practical setting the statement is meant to describe, rendering it true.

SNP heritability is indeed defined as the R² of the optimal linear predictor with known coefficients, yet every polygenic score that researchers compute and publish is obtained from finite GWAS summary statistics, followed by LD clumping or pruning, quality-control thresholds, and (in nearly every pipeline) some form of shrinkage or regularization that deliberately attenuates the coefficients. Consequently the out-of-sample variance explained is bounded strictly below the SNP-heritability ceiling by construction. If the question intended the purely mathematical bound it would have specified “in the infinite-data limit.”

6.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: C4 and C6 are right to insist that the statement must be read against the actual pipeline used to build and validate any PGS. Once we include the mandatory steps—finite-sample effect-size estimation, LD clumping or pruning, QC thresholds, and the shrinkage or regularization that is applied to stabilize out-of-sample performance—the realized R² is bounded strictly below the SNP-heritability ceiling by construction. The mathematical limit in which coefficients are known exactly is admissible in theory but irrelevant to the scores researchers can compute; every operational PGS therefore falls short, making the “necessarily lower” claim true in the setting the question describes. The idealized equality invoked by the False camp would require rewording the statement to “cannot exceed in infinite data,” which is not how it is written.
